Hi Emily —

Great to speak earlier. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

Summary of performance asks we captured on the call:
- Latency target: p95 generation latency <= 200ms for short-response flows (<= 256 tokens)
- Throughput: sustained 120k tokens/min (tokenized) across peak hour bursts
- Concurrency: ability to handle 450 parallel active requests (concurrent HTTP streams) with graceful throttling beyond that
- Streaming: chunked responses for streaming audio transcripts (server-side chunk size ~512 tokens, max idle keepalive 30s)

Immediate asks from CobaltPay that we committed to validate:
1) Whether Redwood can guarantee the 450 parallel active requests under the dedicated tier (or map to equivalent reserved capacity).
2) How connection multiplexing affects per-customer rate limits and whether a single long-lived connection can multiplex N logical streams without counting as N concurrent requests.
3) Proposed rate-limit tiers and uplift pricing for the expected token throughput and concurrency headroom.

What we will do next (for our internal follow-ups I copied Marissa):
- Marissa: produce a short capacity matrix showing how 450 parallel streams maps to queued requests, GPU pools required, and expected p95 under progressive degradation (attached spreadsheet).
- Ben: draft commercial options (rate-limit tiers, burst windows, and a short-term trial uplift).
- Jonas: align on SLO language for the contract and propose a simple fallback policy (lower-capacity model variant + queuing) for overload scenarios.

Proposed timeline: we’ll share the capacity matrix and draft ratecard by EOD Monday PST and schedule a technical Q&A on Tuesday 10am PT. Does that work for you?

1) Concurrency model: our gateway keeps long-lived connections from a small fleet of workers (approx 80 processes). Ideally, we want to multiplex up to 6 logical requests per connection to reduce OS sockets and TCP churn. Will Redwood count each logical stream against the concurrency cap, or count by TCP connection?

2) Streaming constraints: for real-time voice transcripts we need end-to-end latency (client -> model -> client chunk) under 300ms for typical 8k audio segments. That includes our network hop; please call out assumptions in the capacity matrix.

3) Trial: we prefer a 2-week sandbox with a soft quota of 150% of our projected peak so we can validate burst behavior. Any temporary uplift fees should be capped.

Hi Emily —

Thanks for the clear asks. Quick technical clarifications from infra/SE: 

- Concurrency accounting: Redwood counts logical request streams for SLO/rate-limit accounting (not raw TCP sockets). That means a single long-lived connection that multiplexes 6 logical requests will count as 6 concurrent streams against the quota. However, we offer connection pooling optimizations to reduce TLS/handshake overhead while still counting per-logical-stream for fairness.

- Multiplexing: For HTTP/2 or gRPC streams we support multiplexing; recommended configuration is max 6 streams/connection for your worker fleet pattern to avoid head-of-line blocking. We can tune the max per-connection parameter during the trial.

- Degradation policy: Proposed fallback is a staged degradation: 1) Reduce model context/quantize to a faster variant (maintain <400ms p95), 2) Apply 429-style soft throttling with a retry-after and token-based backoff, 3) Redirect low-priority requests to batch endpoints. We’ll include expected p95 numbers for each stage in the matrix.

- Streaming latency assumption: the 300ms E2E target is boundary-pushing; network adds variability. In the capacity matrix I included a conservative 80ms network overhead for a US-based region; if CobaltPay’s workers sit in us-west 2 this should be reasonable. Please confirm your worker region.

I’ve updated the spreadsheet with per-stage p95 estimates (see Drive link) and added a column showing how multiplexing maps to billing units. Drive: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1A2BcX_example

I’ll be on the Tuesday 10am PT call to walk through the capacity matrix.

—Marissa
